This Windows machine was migrated to a Mac on 2026-08-05, but its scheduled tasks
still run nightly and are fighting the Mac over shared git repos — that second
writer is manufacturing repo divergence on the Mac every night. This machine's
~/.claude/scripts/daily-backup.ps1 is now the macOS port, which fails on Windows
(/usr/bin/rsync, wrong DEV path) while logging false "SNAP OK" receipts. Goal:
one final sync, then make this machine a read-only client. Steps:

     $env:USERPROFILE\.claude                  (dotclaude)
     $env:USERPROFILE\.claude\global-memory
     $env:USERPROFILE\.claude\skills
     $env:USERPROFILE\Desktop\SecondBrain
   For EACH, in this order:
   a. Run `git status` and show me the output before changing anything.
   b. If there are dirty or untracked files, show me `git diff` (and for untracked
      files, their first ~30 lines) so I can see what's local-only. Some of these
      exist nowhere else — that's the whole point of this step.
   c. Commit them with a clear message, then `git pull --rebase origin main`,
      then push.
   Expect the "behind" count to be large — the Mac has been the active writer
   since 2026-08-05, so this machine is many commits behind on all four. That is
   normal, not a problem. Rebase conflicts are NOT normal: stop and show me the
   conflicting hunks instead of resolving them.
   Note: plain `git stash` does not pick up UNTRACKED files. If you need to stash
   to pull, use `git stash -u`, or rename the local file aside first.

2. DISABLE THE AUTOMATION (disable, do NOT unregister — RESTORE.md documents
   re-registration if it's ever wanted):
   Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {$_.TaskName -like 'KeystoneOS*' -or
     $_.TaskName -eq 'MorningBriefing'} | Disable-ScheduledTask
   Disabling MorningBriefing here is intended — that job was retired by decision
   on 2026-08-14 and is already shut off on the Mac. Not collateral damage.

   Select-Object TaskName,State` filtered to KeystoneOS*/MorningBriefing — the
   result should be empty. Then confirm all four repos above report clean and
   up to date with origin. From here this machine can still be used normally for
   reading and git work; it just runs no scheduled writers.

conflicts and surprises come to me before you act; do not touch secrets/, .env
files, or credentials.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

through 08-14:

[2026-08-14 07:23] daily-backup: 3 error(s): repo-diverged:SecondBrain,
snapshot:sessions, manifest-unmanaged:...

**What it is.** `snapshot:sessions` comes from `daily-backup.ps1` line 221:

Snapshot "$U/.codex/sessions"   "$P/codex/sessions"   @()

return ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0)

    return ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0 -or $LASTEXITCODE -eq 24)
```

a backup script, and you asked for surprises to come to you.

```

Here's the map. One thing that reframes everything: the services list shows **Intune, Remote Help, Dell Client Management, three Defender components, and GlobalProtect VPN** — this is a corporate-managed machine. A large share of what's running isn't yours to turn off, and attempting it will either fail or get reverted by policy.

Current snapshot, grouped:

| Group | RAM | Disk I/O | Yours to disable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Security / IT-managed | ~735 MB | **32.6 GB** | **No** |
| Cloud sync & backup (×5) | ~570 MB | 21.8 GB | Partly |
| Indexing / search | ~35 MB | 23.3 GB | Partly |
| Your apps | ~6.4 GB | 46 GB | Yes |
| Vendor updaters | ~65 MB | small | Mostly |

---

## 1. Security & IT management — leave alone

**Operating:** `MsMpEng` (Defender Antivirus, 525 MB), `MsSense` (Defender for Endpoint EDR, 210 MB), `MDCoreSvc`, `IntuneManagementExtension`, `Remote Help`, `PanGPS` (Palo Alto GlobalProtect VPN), `DellClientManagementService`, plus the `SoftLanding` scheduled tasks.

**Why:** Your employer pushed them via Intune. They're conditions of the machine being on the network, not choices you made.

**Responsible for:** Real-time file scanning, threat detection and reporting to a central console, policy and software deployment, VPN, remote IT support.

**If turned off:** Defender is your **single largest disk I/O source at 27.8 GB** — more than any app. Turning it off would produce a genuinely noticeable speedup. Don't. It will be re-enabled by policy within hours, may flag your machine as non-compliant, and it's the one category where the tradeoff isn't yours to make unilaterally. The legitimate move is asking IT for a **scan exclusion** on your working folders — that's a normal request for people working with large data files.

## 2. Cloud sync & backup — this is your real redundancy

**Operating:** OneDrive (2 processes, 15 GB I/O), Google Drive FS (5.9 GB), CrashPlan (6 processes, 367 MB, 6.4 GB), Box Update Service, AdobeCollabSync (4.85 GB).

**Why:** Each was installed for a different purpose at a different time and none of them know about the others.

**Responsible for:** Watching your filesystem for changes and uploading them. CrashPlan does continuous versioned backup; the rest do folder sync.

**If turned off:** This is your best real win. Every time you save a large `.xlsx`, it's scanned by Defender, then noticed and uploaded by however many of these watch that folder. **Five systems doing overlapping work is four too many.** You won't lose files by quitting them — they resume and catch up. The question worth answering: *which one is actually your backup of record?* Keep that one plus CrashPlan, quit the rest. AdobeCollabSync in particular does nothing you'd miss.

## 3. Indexing & search

**Operating:** Windows `SearchIndexer` — only 35 MB of RAM but **23.3 GB of disk I/O**, second only to Defender. Plus `Everything` (voidtools), which your `everything-search` skill depends on.

**Why:** SearchIndexer builds the index behind Start-menu and File Explorer search. Everything builds a filename index.

**Responsible for:** Making search instant, by doing the work continuously in advance.

**If turned off:** Search gets slow and falls back to scanning on demand. Everything is very lightweight and worth keeping. SearchIndexer is worth *narrowing* rather than disabling — exclude your big `DEV` and data folders from indexed locations and you keep Start-menu search while dropping most of that 23 GB.

## 4. Your applications — where the RAM actually goes

**Operating:** `msedgewebview2` (69 processes, 1.9 GB), VS Code (13 processes, 1.3 GB), `vmmemWSL` (1,025 MB), Excel (749 MB), Claude (691 MB — me), Wispr Flow (10 processes, 493 MB), R, Grammarly (181 MB).

**Why:** WebView2 is the giveaway — Superhuman, Acrobat, new Outlook, and Teams each embed a full private copy of the Edge browser engine. You're effectively running four extra browsers alongside Chrome.

**Responsible for:** Your actual work. This is the legitimate load.

**If turned off:** Direct, immediate RAM back — this is the only group where quitting things helps instantly and reversibly. Two specifics worth knowing: **WSL grew from 629 MB to 1,025 MB just during this conversation**, which is exactly the uncapped behavior the `.wslconfig` I wrote will stop. And Grammarly plus Wispr Flow together are ~674 MB of always-resident convenience — fine if you use them constantly, expensive if you don't.

## 5. Vendor updaters — safe to trim, small payoff

**Operating:** Adobe ARM + Adobe Update + Creative Cloud, Logi Options+ updater, Zoom Sharing Service, Intel Graphics Service.

**Why:** Every vendor wants a resident process to check for updates.

**Responsible for:** Update checks; Logi Options+ also drives your mouse/keyboard button customizations.

**If turned off:** You update manually instead. Honest assessment: this is ~65 MB and the least valuable thing to fiddle with. Adobe's are the most gratuitous. Don't disable Logi Options+ if you use custom mouse buttons.

---

**The short version:** your security stack costs the most in disk I/O and is the one thing you shouldn't touch. Your apps cost the most in RAM and are entirely yours to manage. The genuine waste is in the middle — five overlapping sync/backup systems and an indexer crawling folders that don't need indexing.

Want me to turn this into a document you can keep and reference later? And I'm happy to help pick which sync clients to retire if you tell me which one holds your real backup.
